strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: using structured FACS Action Unit prompts instead of generic class prompts or noisy LLM descriptions is a sensible and interpretable way to model subtle, low-intensity expressions (pain, stress, ambivalence) that CLIP's generic prompts struggle with.

The two-level design is well articulated: CLIP-AU learns subject-agnostic AU–video alignment with only lightweight trainable components (AU adapter, 1D-CNN temporal module, MLP classifier) while keeping CLIP frozen, and CLIP-AUTT adds subject-level test-time personalization via entropy minimization on AU prompt embeddings, combining temporal window selection with prompt tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: comparisons against recent CLIP-based FER methods (EmoCLIP, X-CLIP, Exp-CLIP) and five image-level plus one video-level TTA baselines across three subtle-ER datasets; subject-wise breakdowns (Tables 2, 3 and supplementary Tables 2–4) directly support the personalization claim; the 'Are Action Units Really Helping?' ablation (46 generic class prompts collapsing under TTA, ~15% drop on StressID) is a convincing control experiment.

Solid ablation coverage: window length sensitivity, CP vs AU vs CP+AU fusion, AU adapter impact (t-SNE analysis), prompt-template selection, and extended key-frame selection analysis; the gradient analysis of entropy minimization in the supplement clarifies why adaptation re-weights AU relevance per subject.

Qualitative validation against an external AU detector (OpenFace) adds credibility to the claim that adapted AU prompts reflect genuine subject-specific facial activations; efficiency/complexity analysis (throughput, trainable params, GFLOPs vs WAR) supports the lightweight design claim.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is a composition of standard components — cosine similarity to text prompts, a lightweight MLP classifier, entropy-minimization TTA (Tent/TPT-style) applied to text prompt embeddings, and low-entropy window selection. The contribution is more of a well-executed adaptation of known techniques to a specific, under-explored problem (subtle video ER personalization) than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Statistical rigor is thin given small evaluation sets: results are averaged over only 10 target subjects per dataset, and perfect 100% scores on several subjects (BioVid Woman-43, StressID Sub-3/Sub-7) are plausible signs of over-adaptation on tiny subject-specific test sets; no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, making the large margins (e.g., BioVid 81.5 vs 76.1 WAR) harder to fully trust.

Results on the BAH dataset are much weaker than the narrative suggests: UAR is essentially at chance (~50.2, same as all baselines) and the F1 gain over the best baseline is marginal (41.1 vs 40.7). This suggests WAR gains on BAH largely exploit class imbalance rather than genuine personalization; the paper should discuss this more prominently.

Fairness of comparisons: image-level TTA baselines (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA) operate on class prompts on frame-level inputs, whereas the proposed method uses AU prompts plus a temporal module trained on source subjects; while the Ens.-CPs TTA control partially addresses this, a stronger control would adapt the same AU-based architecture without window selection, and comparisons with AU-detector-feature pipelines (e.g., OpenFace-based FER) are absent despite OpenFace being used for qualitative validation.

Test-time protocol details are underspecified in the main text: how many videos per subject are used for adaptation, whether predictions on the adapted subject's videos are evaluated on the same videos used for adaptation (transductive setting), and how adaptation/reset interacts with the reported subject-level metrics are not clearly stated; this affects the interpretation of 'personalization'.

Minor presentation issues: typos and grammar errors ('test-time shifty', 'Entopry' in Fig. 3, 'CLIP-AU evaluated on three challenging datasets'), and some notation (z'_{sm} defined via s'_i inconsistently) should be cleaned up; code is promised but not yet publicly available, which limits reproducibility at review time.

strengths: The core idea of using FACS Action Units as structured, interpretable text prompts within CLIP is well-motivated for subtle, low-intensity expressions (pain, stress, ambivalence), and it avoids both LLM-generated prompts and AU ground-truth supervision, which is a sensible and reasonably novel design for this problem setting.

The test-time personalization method (CLIP-AUTT) is thoughtfully tailored to video: entropy-guided temporal window selection addresses the fact that subtle expressions peak only in specific segments, and adapting only the AU prompt embeddings (with encoders and classifier frozen) is a lightweight, stable design choice that reduces drift risk compared to full TTA.

Empirical evaluation is broad: three challenging and heterogeneous datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH), comparison against recent CLIP-based FER methods (EmoCLIP, X-CLIP, Exp-CLIP) and recent TTA methods (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA, T3AL), with both average and per-subject results, WAR/UAR/F1, and efficiency analysis (Fig. 1d).

The ablations are substantive rather than cosmetic: the 'Are Action Units Really Helping?' experiment with a matched 46-prompt class-prompt ensemble (nearly 15% drop under TTA on StressID), CP+AU fusion analysis, AU adapter impact via t-SNE, prompt-template selection, window-length sensitivity, and robustness to increasing target-subject pools all directly probe the central claims.

Qualitative analysis is appropriate for the interpretability claim: predicted AU activations are validated against an external detector (OpenFace), and the BAH failure-mode discussion (overlapping/contradictory AU combinations, over-adaptation on short segments) is an honest limitation, not merely decorative.

Good reproducibility posture: the full 46-AU prompt list, class-prompt templates, target-subject identities, and baseline implementation details are provided in the supplementary material, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate. CLIP-AUTT is essentially Tent-style entropy minimization applied to AU text embeddings plus argmin-entropy window selection; both ingredients (Tent, TPT/PromptAlign) are established, and the paper's framing as a new TTA paradigm overstates what is a well-executed combination tailored to this domain.

Evaluation rigor has concerning gaps. (i) The supplementary per-subject tables report WAR and UAR as numerically identical for every method and subject on BioVid and StressID, which strongly suggests a metric-computation bug or degenerate class structure that is never discussed; (ii) on BAH, UAR hovers at ~50% for all methods, indicating majority-class collapse, which makes the claimed superiority on BAH much weaker than the abstract implies; (iii) results are averaged over only 10 target subjects per dataset with no variance, no multiple seeds, and no significance testing, despite CLIP-AUTT sometimes achieving perfect 100.0 scores that warrant scrutiny for over-adaptation.

The transductive setup deserves more careful treatment. CLIP-AUTT adapts on the very video being classified (10 iterations per video), and while baselines are also adapted per sample, the paper does not report adaptation cost per test video or test the method in a streaming/one-pass setting, limiting the practical claims of 'test-time' applicability.

Some results do not support the strength of the claims: CLIP-AU loses to EmoCLIP† in WAR on StressID (66.5 vs 67.0), individual F1 scores on BAH are often below baselines (e.g., Sub-1: 38.8 vs 45.9), and Table 2 shows CLIP-AUTT at 33.3 F1 on BioVid Sub-3 versus 40–43.5 for baselines — the paper selectively emphasizes wins without a balanced discussion of per-subject regressions.

Generalization is untested beyond the three in-domain datasets; there is no cross-dataset transfer or out-of-distribution experiment, so the claim of learning 'generic, subject-agnostic AU representations' is supported only indirectly through the CP-replacement ablation on the same datasets.

Presentation issues undermine polish: several notation inconsistencies (Eq. 12 defines z'_sm in terms of s'_1..s'_N never formally introduced; Eq. 5 text switches between p_c and p_{m,c}), typos ('test-time shifty', 'entopry', 'CLIP-AU evaluated on three challenging datasets'), and the abstract/contribution wording could more precisely scope what is new versus adapted from prior TTA work.

Societal/ethical considerations for emotion and pain recognition (privacy, potential misuse in affective surveillance, demographic bias across the small subject pools) are not discussed beyond a passing mention of privacy concerns in related work.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: subtle, subject-specific video emotion recognition (pain, stress, ambivalence) is a realistic and underexplored setting compared to macro-emotion FER, and using FACS Action Units as structured, interpretable text prompts in CLIP is a sensible and elegant way to obtain fine-grained semantic cues without AU annotations or LLM-generated descriptions.

CLIP-AUTT is a reasonable and lightweight test-time personalization design: entropy-guided temporal window selection to isolate the most expressive segment before prompt tuning is a thoughtful addition that addresses the temporal nature of subtle expressions, and it distinguishes the work from image-level CLIP TTA methods (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA).

Extensive evaluation across three challenging subtle-ER datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH), with subject-wise breakdowns (Tables 2 and 3, plus supplementary), window-length and prompt-template ablations, a CP-vs-AU ablation ('Are Action Units Really Helping?'), robustness analysis over increasing target pools, and qualitative AU analysis validated against OpenFace activations.

Efficiency is genuinely addressed: CLIP encoders are frozen, only lightweight modules are trained/adapted, and the paper reports throughput/trainable-parameter/GFLOPs analysis (Fig. 1d), positioning the method as a practical alternative to full fine-tuning.

Supplementary materials are thorough: full AU prompt list, class-prompt templates, gradient analysis of the entropy objective for AU prompt tuning, temporal module design analysis, and additional qualitative results, which supports reproducibility (code promised to be released).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are well-established — cosine-similarity prompt matching, entropy minimization (Tent-style), and prompt tuning at test time (TPT). The main contribution is the application and combination of these components with AU prompts and window selection in the subtle-ER/personalization setting; the methodological novelty over PromptAlign/TPT-style pipelines is modest.

Potential degenerate adaptation behavior: on BAH (supplementary Table 4), CLIP-AUTT's UAR is 50.2, essentially identical to all baselines and to chance, while WAR is 69.8 — suggesting the model (and baselines) largely collapse to the majority class on this dataset. The claimed SOTA on BAH (69.8/41.1 vs 67.9/40.7 for T3AL) is therefore marginal and may not reflect meaningful recognition improvement. The paper acknowledges BAH is hardest but does not analyze this collapse.

Some claims and numbers are inconsistent or overstated: the text states 'EmoCLIP†' is slightly higher in WAR on StressID (67.0 vs 66.5), but Table 1 attributes 67.0 to CLIP-ViT-B/32†; CLIP-AU does not beat full fine-tuning on StressID WAR. Also the framing 'without CLIP fine-tuning' is somewhat misleading — CLIP-AU still trains adapter, temporal module, and classifier on labeled source subjects, and CLIP-AUTT uses a source-fine-tuned backbone.

Ambiguity about the novelty boundary: the introduction states 'We first introduced CLIP-AU...', which suggests CLIP-AU may be prior work, leaving CLIP-AUTT as the only new contribution here. This attribution should be clarified; if CLIP-AU is novel to this paper, the phrasing is confusing.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are averaged over only 10 target subjects per dataset, no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and gains such as 81.5 vs 76.1 WAR on BioVid could be sensitive to subject selection. Some perfect scores (100.0 WAR on several subjects) after per-video entropy minimization raise concerns about overconfident collapse rather than genuine personalization.

Only a single video is adapted per subject with resetting, and the entropy objective optimizes directly on the test video; the interaction between window selection and entropy minimization (e.g., selection bias toward easy windows) is not analyzed, and the window ablation is only performed on BioVid.

Minor writing/presentation issues: typos ('entopry', 'test-time shifty'), 'metrics' miswritten as 'matrices' in table captions, and ablation text on p.14 refers to 'Table 4 (left)/(middle)' while Fig. 4 places these panels as sub-figures, which is confusing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: using structured FACS-derived Action Unit phrases as text prompts inside CLIP, enabling fine-grained subtle-expression modeling (pain, stress, ambivalence) without AU ground-truth annotations or LLM-generated prompts, with an interpretable AU–video similarity bottleneck.

The two-stage design is coherent: CLIP-AU learns subject-agnostic AU semantics, and CLIP-AUTT adds video-level test-time personalization via entropy-guided temporal window selection plus AU prompt tuning, addressing a genuinely underexplored setting (video-based, subject-level TTA for subtle ER) as opposed to static-image CLIP TTA.

Comprehensive and transparent experiments: three datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH), subject-wise breakdowns for TTA baselines, ablations on window length, prompt templates, AU vs class prompts (early/late fusion), AU adapter, three-seed robustness, frame-sampling rates, phrase- vs sentence-level prompts, an additional FERV39K evaluation, and an efficiency/throughput analysis.
Honest discussion of limitations, notably the over-adaptation risk on ambivalent expressions in BAH and the admission that AU prompt tuning is the main driver over window selection (Table 5).
The supplementary derivation of the entropy gradient w.r.t. AU embeddings (Sec. 1) gives useful insight into why prompt tuning re-weights subject-relevant AUs.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a substantive concern: TTA baselines use the CLIP-ViT-B/32† backbone, while CLIP-AUTT builds on the stronger CLIP-AU source model. Part of the reported TTA gains may stem from the stronger source model rather than the personalization method itself. Ablating CLIP-AUTT's components on top of an identical source backbone to the baselines would strengthen the claim.

Evaluation scale is limited: only 10 target subjects per dataset, and multi-seed robustness is reported for StressID only. Given the variance visible in subject-wise tables, confidence intervals or significance tests over subjects/runs would be needed to support 'sets a new state of the art' claims.

On BAH, CLIP-AUTT's UAR is 50.2% (chance for the binary setting) and essentially identical to all baselines; WAR gains may largely reflect majority-class bias rather than genuine recognition. The paper acknowledges this but the headline BAH improvement (69.8/41.1) should be interpreted with this caveat.

Several AU-to-description mappings appear inconsistent with standard FACS (e.g., AU-06 is cheek raiser, AU-07 lid tightener, AU-09 nose wrinkler, AU-25 lips part, whereas the paper's Table 1 assigns 'eyelids tightened' to AU-06, 'nose wrinkled' to AU-07, 'eyes slitted' to AU-25). If the prompt semantics deviate from FACS, this should be justified or corrected, as it affects interpretability claims.

Deployment practicality of per-video test-time adaptation (10 gradient iterations per video, batch size 1) is discussed qualitatively but the trade-off of adaptation cost per subject/video at inference is not fully analyzed relative to the promised efficiency.

Novelty is moderate: the ingredients (entropy minimization, prompt tuning, temporal windowing) are combinations of established techniques (TPT, T3AL, Tent-style objectives); the main originality lies in AU-structured prompting and the video personalization framing, which some reviewers may view as incremental.

Presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is empty ('Our code:'), and there are multiple typos ('test-time shifty', 'entopry', 'a improve', 'matrices' used for 'metrics'), which slightly undermine polish; reproducibility depends on promised supplementary details that are only partially specified (e.g., AU adapter architecture, learning rate schedule for test-time tuning).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well structured, with the two-stage design (subject-agnostic CLIP-AU followed by test-time personalization CLIP-AUTT) logically motivated by the subject-specific variability of subtle expressions.

Using Action Units as structured textual prompts is an interpretable alternative to LLM-generated prompts, and the ablation showing class prompts collapse under TTA (Table 4 right) supports the core design claim.

Evaluation covers three datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) plus a FERV39K sanity check in the supplement, with extensive ablations on window length, prompt templates, CP-vs-AU prompts, AU adapter, and component contributions (Table 5), including seed-robustness analysis for StressID.
Efficiency analysis (Fig. 1d) and the fairness discussion of window selection vs. T3AL (suppl. 3.7b) show awareness of confounds in TTA comparisons.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: CLIP-AU is essentially frozen-CLIP AU text prompts + cosine-similarity features + a small classifier, and CLIP-AUTT is entropy minimization on prompt embeddings (closely following TPT) plus minimum-entropy window selection; both are incremental combinations of known components applied to a niche problem, and the paper itself acknowledges prior AU-prompting work.

Results on BAH are near-chance and barely support the SOTA claims: all TTA baselines and CLIP-AUTT have UAR ~50.0 (Table 4 suppl.), and F1 improves only from 39.7/40.7 to 41.1. Framing this as 'outperforming state-of-the-art' overstates marginal differences.

Several subject-level results appear degenerate: BioVid Sub-3 and Sub-8 stay at 50.0 WAR for every method, with F1 of 33.3 for CLIP-AUTT, suggesting tiny per-subject test sets or collapsed predictions; the paper does not discuss this. With only 10 target subjects and no confidence intervals or significance testing in the main tables, the headline gains (e.g., StressID F1 77.9 vs 59.4) are hard to verify.

The adaptation procedure has a confirmation-bias risk the paper does not address: the minimum-entropy window of the same test video is used to tune the AU prompts, which are then used to classify that same video, with no anti-collapse mechanism or augmentation (unlike TPT). This makes the large StressID gains potentially an artifact of aggressive per-video transductive tuning rather than genuine personalization.

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract's code link is an empty placeholder ('Our code:'), key adaptation hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer steps per video, window length used for final results on StressID/BAH) are underspecified, and several notation inconsistencies (Eq. 12 uses z'_sm vs s'_i) hinder faithful reimplementation.

Presentation quality issues undermine polish: typos in Fig. 3 ('entopry', 'a improve'), a reference to 'Figure 4 (right)' that is actually Table 4, contradictory descriptions of AU meanings across figures (AU-06 labeled 'cheek raiser' in Sec. 1 but 'eyelids tightened' in Fig. 4), and a 'pretraining' stage consisting of only 10 epochs that is never fully characterized.

The comparison of TTA baselines designed for image classification (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA) on video FER may disadvantage them; while T3AL is adapted, the fairness of these protocol choices is not thoroughly validated, and the class counts / label definitions per dataset are never clearly stated in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: subject-specific test-time personalization for subtle, fine-grained video emotion recognition (pain/stress/ambivalence), an area where standard CLIP-based FER methods perform poorly.

The core idea of using FACS Action Units as structured, interpretable textual prompts (without AU annotations or LLM-generated text) is well-motivated, clearly articulated, and technically sound; the analysis of the entropy gradient w.r.t. AU embeddings in the supplement nicely explains the adaptation mechanism.

Comprehensive experiments across three challenging video ER datasets with subject-wise breakdowns, efficiency analysis (Fig. 1d), and extensive ablations (window length, prompt design, CP vs. AU prompts, adapter impact, temporal module choice, seeds robustness, frame sampling) — the supplementary material substantiates the main claims well.
The method is lightweight (frozen CLIP, small trainable footprint) with reported throughput/parameter/GFLOPs advantages over competing TTA methods.

Consistent improvements over strong TTA baselines on BioVid and StressID (e.g., +5.4/+5.1 WAR/F1 on BioVid, +4.9/+18.5 F1 on StressID), with per-subject tables showing broad gains rather than cherry-picked subjects.
weaknesses: Evidence of class collapse on BAH: CLIP-AUTT's UAR is 50.2 (essentially chance/majority) and its WAR gains over baselines are small; in fact most baselines also sit near 50 UAR, suggesting all methods largely predict the majority class there. The paper acknowledges this only briefly in the supplement; it weakens the claim that AU personalization generalizes across settings.

High per-subject variance: some subjects remain at chance (e.g., BioVid Sub-3/Sub-8 at 50.0 WAR), and several gains are within ranges that could arise from run-to-run variation; statistical significance testing is only provided for one dataset (StressID, 3 seeds), not for Table 1 or the BAH results.

Baseline fairness concerns: image-based TTA methods (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA) were not designed for video/temporal settings; adaptation choices (e.g., frame subsampling for these baselines, the fine-tuned backbone used for each baseline) are described only at a high level and could materially affect the comparison. The EmoCLIP†, X-CLIP, Exp-CLIP comparisons also appear re-implemented, but re-implementation details are thin.

The 'Our code:' link in the abstract is empty, and key hyperparameters of test-time adaptation (number of iterations are given, but learning rate, augmentation policy for CLIP-AUTT, stopping criteria) are incompletely specified, hurting reproducibility.

Some minor issues: typos ('entopry', 'shifty', 'two settings' phrasing, 'matrices' for metrics), Table 5 formatting, and the abstract/introduction overlap in content; a brief Limitations and societal-impact discussion (FER bias, healthcare misuse, privacy) is missing from the main paper despite the sensitive application domains.
The component analysis (Table 5) shows window selection contributes little (0.7 WAR alone), so the headline contribution rests mainly on AU prompt tuning; the paper could be more upfront about this.

AU descriptions appear hand-crafted and, in the qualitative figures, do not always correspond to standard FACS definitions (e.g., AU-06 described as 'eyelids tightened', AU-25 as 'eyes slitted'), which raises questions about prompt quality and interpretation claims; a sensitivity analysis over AU prompt phrasing beyond the sentence-level ablation would help.
